A user prefers AWS OpenSearch because they don't have to pay for basic features like security and alerts. They say teams get the whole Elastic experience 'without the weird nickle and diming' they associate with Elastic's licensing.

From experience with managers, developers and sysadmins: 'No one wants Elastic Search over Open Search... Everyone hates the support and enterprise licensing model.' They already pay for AWS support, so they see no reason to add another vendor.

An interim engineering manager noticed most engineers said 'elastic' or 'elasticsearch' in standup. It turned out they had moved to AWS OpenSearch but still used the old name, which the manager read as a sign of the strength of the Elastic brand.

A team that talks with many security teams reports that new projects generally prefer OpenSearch because of openness, and they see many migrations, e.g. at MSPs. Another commenter says most new installs they see in the security industry lean toward OpenSearch rather than Elasticsearch.

'Too late, the community all moved over to OpenSearch. I'll never forgive Elastic for locking basic security features behind their paid licence.' The commenter believes many instances were left exposed on the public internet because auth was not enabled by default.

A consultant uses elastic.co as their #1 example of a vague website: no client, even tech-savvy ones, could say what the company provides. They criticize the pricing model and support. They say the documentation assumes in-depth prior knowledge of the services and server infrastructure.

'We just deployed a new project with OpenSearch after learning from an Elastic salesperson that their licensing fees would eat up significant portions of the projects profits.' They also suspect much vital functionality is still behind a subscription because it isn't spelled out clearly.

A user is happy that Elastic kept the Elastic License option alongside AGPL. They say it still lets them self-host if the vendor folds or raises prices, fix bugs, and add features, and only bars building a direct hosted competitor. They find this less restrictive in practice than AGPL.
Two approaches to Elasticsearch security in production: upgrade to a paid Elastic cluster and use its security suite, or put a reverse proxy like nginx in front of Elastic to handle security.
Tuning tip: the default refresh interval is 1 second. Increase it if your application allows, and for bulk indexing consider disabling it outright to speed up indexing.

A commenter points to Aphyr's Jepsen analysis showing Elasticsearch could lose indexed documents during network partitions on an older version. They don't fully trust the resiliency docs given past handling of such issues: 'Elastic is great as a search index, not as a primary database.'
'I found Elastic Cloud on K8s to be the best way to deploy and manage Elastic clusters on Kubernetes so far.' The operator uses CRDs and handles deployments, statefulsets and upgrades declaratively.

A user runs Elasticsearch in a Kubernetes StatefulSet and says it works nicely out of the box using headless Services for node discovery. A custom preStop hook blocks shutdown until the cluster is GREEN, so it doesn't go RED when a node stops.

Users found Elastic's subscription tiers and security documentation confusing. The subscriptions page didn't clearly explain what 'File and Native Authentication' meant, while older docs still said there was no security and anyone who could reach the cluster was effectively a superuser.
'Elastic's SaaS offering is incredibly expensive vs AWS Elasticsearch.'
Having used AWS Elasticsearch, a user says it 'has a lot of deep problems with it in its current state so Elastic can compete on value just fine.'

Elastic's proprietary add-ons in its cloud and subscription tiers include machine learning, APM, endpoint security, threat detection and fine-grained access control. 'Unfortunately for them a lot of users don't need any of that, and are just fine with the formerly-OSS core.'
Contrast with AWS: 'The AWS version of ES has been abysmal- it's only saving grace is that it's "in the ecosystem"... Never again.'

'While I really want to support Elastic here we are likely going to have to move to Amazon's Apache-licensed fork for our internal use because SSPL is incompatible with our company's open source policy.'

A commenter notes Elastic is not just a database engine but a whole ecosystem: drivers, tooling, existing code, data pipelines, documentation and tutorials. They argue this makes keeping a fork current over the long term challenging.
